summary: Wildfires are an escalating threat across South America, causing devastating biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation, greenhouse gas emissions, and socioeconomic damage. Anticipating fire activity remains a major challenge for governments and emergency management agencies, which often lack accessible tools to understand historical fire patterns and anticipate periods of unusually high fire activity. FIRECHRON addresses this challenge by transforming over 25 years of NASA satellite observations into actionable fire intelligence. The platform combines harmonised MODIS and VIIRS data, an interactive historical calendar, regional news, and comparative visualisations to help users explore fire patterns and understand their context. Additionally, its AI-powered forecasting model estimates the probability of unusually high fire activity up to three months ahead, helping identify regions that may require greater attention and supporting more informed prevention and resource allocation decisions. By connecting historical insights with predictive capabilities, FIRECHRON aims to make wildfire intelligence more accessible and help communities prepare for what lies ahead.
details:
Summary

Firechron is a platform developed as part of the NASA Space Apps Challenge in Mendoza that integrates more than 25 years of satellite observations of fire activity in South America. Its main objective is to bridge the gaps between the MODIS and VIIRS sensors to build a consistent time series, facilitate the analysis of temporal and spatial patterns, and provide the monitoring and forecasting tools that contribute to fire management.

The project processes millions of heat source detections obtained from NASA FIRMS between November 2000 and November 2026, derived from five satellites: Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21.

Following a process of data cleaning, standardization, and harmonization, an interactive web application was developed. It allows users to explore historical trends in fire activity, identify seasonal patterns, compare current periods with historical records, and view geographic information. Additionally, a predictive model was developed to estimate, up to three months in advance, whether a region is likely to experience higher-than-usual fire activity.

Benefits and Advantages

Firechron offers several advantages over the isolated use of conventional satellite data:

  • Historical continuity: it integrates more than 25 years of observations from different sensors, reducing the artificial discontinuities caused by instrumental differences.
  • Regional comparability: it uses specific correction factors for different geographic regions, improving the consistency of the records.
  • Accessibility: it transforms large volumes of satellite data into intuitive visualisations, without requiring advanced knowledge of geospatial processing
  • Flexible analysis: it allows users to select any area of interest and study its historical, seasonal, and spatial behaviour.
  • Predictive capability: incorporates a seasonal forecast 3 months in advance, providing additional information for planning.
  • Open data and reproducibility: facilitates the reuse of data and methodology through open-source code, public sources, and documentation (code is published on GitHub).
  • Data displayed in the application can be downloaded in CSV format, allowing users to reuse the information as input for other tools, platforms, and analytical workflows.

Unique and Creative Aspects

The key creative aspect of Firechron is the integration of different satellite sources into a single, comparable time series, using a harmonization methodology that accounts for instrumental and geographic differences. The project transforms millions of records into an interactive calendar that allows users to interpret patterns of fire activity over more than two decades.

Another innovative aspect is the combination of historical analysis with a seasonal forecast model. In this way, the application not only helps users understand what happened but also explore whether an upcoming season might see higher-than-usual activity.

The incorporation of regional correction factors is a key feature, as it recognizes that differences between sensors are not uniform across the continent and require spatially differentiated treatment.

Finally, the bilingual, open-source approach aims to ensure that the results can be used, replicated, and expanded upon by various communities and institutions.

Visual Identity: The FIRECHRON logo is an original custom vector artwork created manually in Adobe Illustrator by our team; no AI tools were used to generate or modify logos or brand marks.

Expected Impact

The intended impact of Firechron is to facilitate access to historical and predictive information on wildfire activity in South America, improving understanding of temporal and spatial patterns.

The platform is designed for researchers, environmental agencies, fire management officials, public institutions, and anyone interested in studying wildfire activity in a specific region.

By identifying seasons of heightened activity, comparing current conditions with historical records, and providing seasonal forecasts, Firechron aims to provide information that can be used to anticipate periods requiring greater attention, guide resource planning, and support decision-making.

The project does not intend to replace official fire detection or warning systems, but rather to complement them with harmonized historical data and accessible analytical tools.

Tools and Technologies Used

The development of FIRECHRON combines data processing, geospatial analysis, machine learning, and web development and deployment technologies. The main tools and technologies used include:

  • Python: The primary programming language used throughout the project, supporting data processing, analysis, model development, and application implementation.
    • Pandas and NumPy: Core libraries for data manipulation and numerical computing. NumPy provides efficient mathematical operations and numerical array processing, while Pandas offers tools for handling and analyzing tabular data. Both were essential for processing satellite observations from MODIS and VIIRS, as well as climate datasets from ERA5.
    • Streamlit: Used to develop the web application, enabling the implementation of interactive interfaces and data-driven visualizations directly in Python.
    • Plotly: Used to create interactive charts, maps, and visualizations for exploring historical fire activity and forecasting results.
    • Requests: Used to communicate with external APIs and retrieve data from sources such as ERA5 and NASA FIRMS.
    • DuckDB: An analytical database engine designed for efficient SQL queries over large datasets. It was particularly useful for querying and aggregating large Parquet files without requiring the entire dataset to be loaded into memory.

Factors Considered by the Team

Throughout the development of FIRECHRON, several factors were considered to ensure that the results were comparable, representative, and useful.

Instrumental and Observation Factors

  • Differences in spatial resolution between MODIS and VIIRS.
  • Differences in sensor characteristics and detection confidence levels.
  • Temporal continuity of observations and transitions between satellites.
  • Differences between historical and Near Real-Time (NRT) products.

Geographic Factors

  • Spatial variability in detection differences between sensors.
  • Spatial resolution and data aggregation strategies.
  • Preservation of the geographic location of detections.

Temporal Factors

  • Seasonality of fire activity.
  • Interannual variability.
  • Comparison of historical reference periods.

Methodological and Reliability Factors

  • Identification and removal of duplicate records.
  • Selection of detections according to their confidence levels.
  • Exclusion of persistent heat sources.
  • Separation of datasets used for training, validation and testing.
  • Comparison of predictive model outputs against historical reference baselines.
  • Recognition of the limitations of satellite detections, since a detected thermal anomaly does not necessarily correspond to a confirmed wildfire.

Future Developments

  • A model for identifying causes based on population density data and news articles linked to the date and location of the search.
  • Verify the inclusion of information on cloud cover, vegetation, and humidity to improve the quality of fire predictions.
  • Increase the temporal resolution of the data to enable predictions to provide information on the daily evolution of events rather than just reporting average monthly behaviour.
  • Train a neural network using time series data to improve predictions.
